meta.title: Install ai-jail and run your first jailed agent
meta.description: Install ai-jail with Homebrew, the AUR, cargo or Nix, preview the sandbox with a dry run, then start Claude Code or Codex with only the network and its login.

hero.title: Install it, look inside, run your agent
hero.lede: ai-jail is one program with no daemon and no root. You install it, put its name in front of the command you already type, and the agent starts inside a sandbox.

install.title: Install
install.lede: Choose the way you already install command line tools. Every method gives you the same single ai-jail program.
notes: Works on macOS and on Linux.
The first package is a prebuilt binary for Linux x86_64. The second builds from source.
Needs a Rust toolchain. --locked builds with the dependency versions the release was tested with.
The first line runs an agent without installing anything. The second installs for your user. The flake points ai-jail at its own copy of bubblewrap.
The archives are signed, with checksums next to them. Unpack one and put ai-jail somewhere on your PATH. How to check the signature is on the Security page.

items.title: Linux
items.text: Install bubblewrap, the small program ai-jail uses to build the sandbox. Most distributions package it as bubblewrap.

items.title: macOS
items.text: Nothing to install. ai-jail uses sandbox-exec, which ships with macOS. Apple marks that interface as deprecated.

items.title: Windows
items.text: Not supported. Use WSL2 and follow the Linux steps inside it.

first.title: Your first run
first.lede: Three commands take you from a plan, to a look inside, to a working agent. ai-jail opens nothing until you ask.
first.alt: Three panels from left to right. Dry run: the cell is only a dashed outline and the agent waits outside. Look around: the cell is solid and holds a terminal and the project folder. Run the agent: the agent and the project are inside, with two openings in the wall, one for the network and one for the agent's login. Your home folder stays barred outside in all three.
first.caption: Your home directory stays outside at every step. Only the last step opens anything, and only the two things a cloud agent needs.

steps.title: See the plan without running anything
steps.text: Go to your project and ask for a dry run. ai-jail prints the sandbox command it would use and exits. A dry run never writes a file.

steps.title: Look around inside
steps.text: Start a plain shell in the jail. Your project is there at its real path and you can edit it. Your home directory is a fresh, empty one, and your shell's tokens are gone. Type exit to leave.

steps.title: Run the agent with the two things it needs
steps.text: An agent that talks to a cloud model needs the network to reach it, and its own saved login to prove who you are. Both are off by default, so you turn them on: --network and --agent-state. Since version 1.22, ai-jail prints a warning naming the missing flag if you start a known agent without one of them.

steps.title: Make it the default for that agent
steps.text: Put the two settings in ~/.ai-jail, your own config file, under the agent's name. After that the short command is enough. The .ai-jail file that may appear in the project can only tighten the jail. It can never turn the network or a login on, so a repository you clone cannot open the jail for itself.

gitignore.title: The .ai-jail file in your project
gitignore.text: An ordinary run may save project settings to .ai-jail. ai-jail never writes values you pass with --env to it. The agent sees that file as empty. The README suggests adding .ai-jail to .gitignore so git status stays clean inside the jail. Configure explains both config files.

exposure.title: What those two flags give away
exposure.text: --network is the whole network with no per-site filter, so anything the agent can read, it can send. --agent-state lets everything in the jail use that agent's login. Your SSH keys, cloud credentials and other projects are still not there to be read. Security has the full list of limits.

see.title: What you will see inside
see.lede: The prompt changes to (jail) and the project is where it always was. The things worth stealing are missing.
comments: # the project is at its real path
# a token exported in your shell did not come along
# your keys are not in this home
# the jail has its own hostname
see.note: This is a Linux session. macOS has no way to build a separate file tree, so there the same paths exist and reading them is refused.
see.alt: The view from inside the cell. The agent sits next to a large, bright project folder, with an empty home and the system tools behind it. Outside the bars, dim and barred: SSH keys, cloud logins, other projects and the network.
see.caption: From inside, the project is the only thing of yours that exists. The network stays outside too until you pass --network.

trouble.title: If it does not start
trouble.lede: These are the cases the README's troubleshooting covers, plus the two setup rules people trip on.

items.title: bwrap: setting up uid map: Permission denied
items.text: Ubuntu 24.04 and later and Debian 13 and later ship an AppArmor policy that stops programs from creating user namespaces without root, which is how bubblewrap isolates the jail. It affects every rootless tool of this kind. Relax it for the whole system:
items.alt: Or keep the policy and exempt only bwrap. Save this as /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap, then run sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap.

items.title: Your BWRAP_BIN is refused
items.text: You can point ai-jail at a specific bubblewrap with BWRAP_BIN. ai-jail accepts it only when it resolves to a program owned by root that other users cannot write, or to one in a standard multi-user /nix/store. It refuses a copy in your own home, because anyone who can replace that file controls the jail.

items.title: mise tools are missing inside
items.text: ai-jail activates mise when it finds it, but the fresh home has neither mise's config nor its installed tools, so it skips activation. Map both in, read only, from your own config:

items.title: Failed to create stream fd at startup
items.text: This comes from a login script on Ubuntu desktop during mise setup. It is harmless and mise still works. Pass --no-mise to skip mise setup and the message with it.

agents.title: Per agent
agents.lede: ai-jail knows where each agent keeps its login. --agent-state mounts only the folders of the agent you start, and only if they exist.
head: You run
--agent-state mounts
Good to know

notes.claude: For a second Claude profile, point --claude-dir at its directory.
notes.codex: After you resize the window, ai-jail sends Codex a redraw key so the screen repaints.
notes.aimemory: ai-jail recognizes the agent that ai-memory launches and applies that agent's settings, with both programs in one jail.

agents.more: The same works for crush, grok, jcode, pi, aider, soulforge, omp and the kimi commands. Any other command runs too. It gets the same jail and no login folder.
